name: Fucina (Zig tensor runtime and LLM inference engine)
baseline: llama.cpp CPU backend (ggml kernels, llama-bench with -ngl 0), same GGUF file and thread count
workload: Prompt prefill (pp) and decode (tg) tokens per second for Qwen3 0.6B/1.7B, Qwen3.5, Qwen3-30B-A3B MoE and Gemma-4-26B-A4B GGUF models in several quantizations, CPU-only on both sides, paired same-machine runs over many prompt lengths.
claimed_speedup: Apple M1 Max (8 threads): of 236 paired sweep cells Fucina is faster in 221, at parity in 13 and llama.cpp is faster in 2 (BENCHMARK.md headline); dense prefill geomeans 1.18-1.81x per format; Qwen3-30B-A3B MoE prefill 1.44-2.09x; dense decode Q4_K_M/Q4_K_S +15%, Q8_0 +14%. Intel i9-13950HX (AVX2+VNNI): dense Qwen3-0.6B quantized medians 1.32-1.95x. llama.cpp wins: Qwen3.5-0.8B Q8_0 pp32 0.86x, 30B Q6_K decode 0.88x, MoE decode 0.90-0.95x, Q5_K dense decode 0.90x, Gemma-4-26B pp1-9 0.85-0.99x.
compiler_and_flags: Fucina: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast with the default native target (no -Dtarget). llama.cpp build 30af6e2 pinned in tools/fetch_refs.sh; the x86 build was verified as GGML_BLAS=OFF, GGML_NATIVE=ON (-march=native), GGML_LLAMAFILE=ON, GGML_CPU_REPACK=ON, GGML_OPENMP=ON (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE not stated); on the M1 run llama.cpp keeps its default Accelerate BLAS backend.
hardware: Apple M1 Max (arm64, 8 threads, macOS) and Intel Core i9-13950HX (Raptor Lake 8P+16E, AVX2 + AVX-VNNI, no AVX-512, Linux)
tradeoffs: CPU-first runtime written in pure Zig (needs Zig 0.16); covers GGUF Qwen3, Qwen3.5 and Gemma-4 families plus training, speculative decoding and ASR/TTS runners; llama.cpp still wins several MoE decode and small-batch cells.
caveats: Author-run, first-party record with one dated snapshot (2026-07-04) against a pinned llama.cpp build, so results age as llama.cpp advances. On the M1 llama.cpp's Accelerate/AMX path switches on at batch >= 32 and the document says that transition costs it heavily at pp32-129 (up to 7.2x at f16 pp32), so part of the prefill win is a llama.cpp threshold effect. Laptop thermals and page cache move results by several percent; some cells are same-day reruns after a 2026-07-10 scheduler fix. llama.cpp CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE and compiler version are not stated in the document.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/simd?l=zig topic page, then the README Performance section and docs/BENCHMARK.md
why_faster: Author attributes wins to its own CPU kernels and scheduling (for example phased-chain MoE scheduling and f32-accumulate f16 GEMM) and, on M1, to llama.cpp's cost at the Accelerate/AMX switch; no language-level mechanism is claimed.

name: zroar (Zig serialized Roaring bitmaps)
baseline: CRoaring 5.0.0 (roaring64 API, portable and frozen serialization)
workload: CRoaring's benchmark suite ported to Zig plus warm-open and cold-open variants and a zipfian OLTP synthetic dataset: contains, insert, remove, random access, set operations, cardinality, serialize and deserialize; 360 benchmark cases.
claimed_speedup: By design zroar performs 2x to 9x faster (geometric mean) than CRoaring on warm and cold opens and is faster in 339 of 360 cases; real data with bitmaps in memory 2.20x (36 tests), cold open 6.92x vs portable and 3.44x vs frozen (40 tests), synthetic operations 2.18x (132 tests), serialize plus deserialize 615x vs portable (56 tests), cardinality 4.8x geomean. CRoaring decisively wins (about 3x) on random interleaved insert/remove.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0, ReleaseFast; CRoaring 5.0.0 is compiled by the same zig build through addCSourceFiles with the croaringFlags helper in build.zig (AVX-512 toggled from target features), not by CRoaring's own CMake -O3 build.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X, performance governor, frequency fixed at 4.00 GHz, SMT on, benchmark process pinned to one core
tradeoffs: 64-bit integers only; no run container; does not read or write CRoaring's portable serialization format; random interleaved insert/remove is about 3x slower than CRoaring; pre-1.0 with calendar versioning and a format-version check.
caveats: Author benchmark of the author's own library. Much of the cold-open gain comes from the design (a serialized buffer usable without deserialization) rather than from Zig. Datasets built to showcase run containers were excluded because zroar has none. CRoaring is built through Zig's C toolchain, so its flags differ from an upstream CMake build. 27 commits in total, created August 2026. Headline figures are from the README; BENCHMARKS.md (also opened) holds the per-dataset ratio tables.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/compression?l=zig style Zig topic pages, then the zroar README and BENCHMARKS.md
why_faster: README 'Why Is It Faster': one contiguous buffer used in place with few dependent loads, versus CRoaring reaching a container through a chain of dependent loads and an adaptive radix tree index for the high 48 bits.

name: bitdp (compile-time derived bit-parallel alignment kernels)
baseline: edlib (C++), ksw2 extz2_sse (C) and parasail scan16/diag16 (C)
workload: Edit-distance and other linear-gap global alignment of independent DNA pairs (1 kbp and 150 bp sets, real Illumina reads, a 32-guide CRISPR scan of E. coli K-12), measured in GCUPS on one core with every tool's total cost cross-checked.
claimed_speedup: Batched bitdp is faster than edlib, ksw2 and parasail's correct kernels on every DNA workload measured: 35.2 GCUPS against 21.7 (edlib), 2.2 (ksw2) and 5.2 (parasail) for edit distance on 1 kbp pairs with AVX2; margin over edlib shrinks to 15% on real Illumina reads; CRISPR-style scan 0.30 s against 13.3 s for the plain DP. BLOSUM62 is several times slower than parasail.
compiler_and_flags: bitdp built with Zig 0.16.0 -Doptimize=ReleaseFast, once with -Dcpu=znver4 (AVX-512, 8 lanes) and once for AVX2; ksw2 commit 289609b built with gcc 15.2.0 -O3 -march=native; edlib and parasail are Ubuntu builds (flags not stated; the Ubuntu parasail has no AVX-512 kernels).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 8840U (Zen 4, AVX-512), Ubuntu under WSL2 (kernel 6.6.114.1), one core, no threading
tradeoffs: Research code, not yet stable; global and search modes with linear gap costs only; at most 32 distinct score differences and 24 substitution costs; compile-time derivation takes seconds to about 15 s (375 MB of compiler memory for BLOSUM62); batched mode needs many independent pairs to fill SIMD lanes.
caveats: Single author, single machine. The comparison is batched SIMD lanes (one alignment per lane) against single-pair tools, a different regime from edlib's per-pair banded algorithm; bitdp reaches only 0.73-1.20 of the closest hand-derived tool BGSA. Library baselines are distro builds. parasail's striped kernels were excluded because they returned wrong costs on some pairs. Headline figures are from the README Speed section; bench/RESULTS.md (also opened) holds the full tables (35.20 vs 21.73 edlib, 2.20 ksw2, 5.19 parasail scan16 on the 5,000-pair 1 kbp set).
why_faster: Bit-parallel kernel derived at compile time from the recurrence (14 word operations per column for unit edit costs versus 15 for Myers) with one alignment per SIMD lane for independent pairs.

name: z-fasta (Zig FASTA indexer and extractor)
baseline: samtools faidx 1.24 (C, htslib 1.24); report also lists fastahack (C++), seqkit, noodles, rust-bio and pyfaidx
workload: Whole-command wall time for building a samtools-compatible .fai index of GRCh38 (~2.9 GiB), GENCODE v46 transcripts (~459 MiB) and the UniProt human proteome (~13 MiB), plus extracting one 1 kbp region; warm cache, 5 samples after 3 warmups.
claimed_speedup: Index (.fai): 0.3824 s vs 8.1614 s for samtools on the human genome (21.3x, derived from page data), 0.1546 s vs 1.7112 s on the transcriptome (11.1x, derived), 0.0113 s vs 0.0650 s on the proteome (5.8x, derived); 1 kbp GET: 2.3 ms vs 8.2 ms (genome), 8.2 ms with .zfi (28.3 ms with .fai) vs 301.8 ms (transcriptome), 2.7 ms vs 17.9 ms (proteome).
compiler_and_flags: z-fasta v0.3.5 built with Zig 0.16.0 -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dstrip=true (x86_64-linux). samtools 1.24 and htslib 1.24 built from source by tools/install.sh (compiler flags not stated); runner zebrac 0.6.2.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X, Linux, warm page cache (2026-10-10)
tradeoffs: Single static executable covering index, get, validate and stats for FASTA only (not a samtools replacement); the default .zfi index is its own format (side table for ragged wrapping) while --emit-fai writes samtools-compatible .fai.
caveats: First-party benchmark by the author on one host. Each command includes process start, which matters for the small files. The .fai mode is the like-for-like lane; the faster .zfi lane writes a different index. samtools was built by the author with default flags that the report does not list. Repository is a few weeks old. Provenance (Zig and samtools versions, warm-cache protocol, tool install script) is in bench/index/REPORT.md and bench/README.md, both opened.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/bioinformatics?l=zig topic page, then the README Performance section and bench/index/REPORT.md

name: mosdepth (Nim BAM/CRAM depth calculator)
baseline: samtools depth (C, htslib); README table also lists bedtools genomecov (C++) and sambamba depth (D)
workload: Per-base depth on a 30X whole-genome BAM/CRAM with one thread, 500-base window mean depth with three threads, and an exome BAM against 1,195,764 exons.
claimed_speedup: Per-base depth about 2x as fast as samtools depth (BAM: mosdepth 25:23 vs samtools 50:12, relative 1.98; CRAM samtools 1.79x slower); sambamba 5.71x and bedtools 5.31x slower; window depth genome-wide in under 9 minutes of user time with 3 threads (8:44, relative 0.34); exome in 1 minute 38 seconds on one CPU.
compiler_and_flags: Nim with --mm:refc required; build comment in nim.cfg: nim c -a -d:static -d:release mosdepth.nim with htslib built --with-libdeflate. Build flags of samtools and bedtools are not stated.
tradeoffs: Memory is about 32 bits times the longest chromosome (about 1 GB for chr1, against 27 MB for samtools); slower than samtools for small one-off regional queries; no gain past about 4 threads; links htslib (C) for decoding.
caveats: Tier B rests on the peer-reviewed paper cited by the README, which I did not open (publisher blocked); the table in the README lists no hardware or tool versions. Results date from 2017-2018 era samtools and htslib. mosdepth's default skips samtools-style mate-overlap correction unless enabled, and the accuracy check compared samtools depth defaults against mosdepth without overlap detection. The speedup is algorithmic, not a Nim-versus-C effect.
why_faster: README: depth is kept in an array that is incremented at each read start and decremented at its end, summed cumulatively at output; no extra allocations or objects, whereas samtools depth goes through the pileup machinery.

name: sambamba (D tools for SAM/BAM)
baseline: samtools (view, flagstat, markdup, sort, index; C, htslib)
workload: BAM view, flagstat, markdup, sort and index runs of the sambamBench-nf pipeline (Nextflow, about 4 GB test BAM) on a single node with 16 CPUs and 120 GB RAM.
claimed_speedup: README: flagstat 1.4x faster than samtools; markdup almost 6x faster; view 4x faster; index similar; sort beaten by samtools in general, but sambamba is up to 2x faster on large-RAM machines (120GB+).
compiler_and_flags: LDC (LLVM D compiler) 1.6.1 or later preferred; release build with meson (D_LD=gold CC=gcc meson build --buildtype release); samtools version and build flags in the CRG report not read.
hardware: CRG cluster node with 16 CPUs and 120 GB RAM (CPU model not stated)
stars_or_usage: 613 stars; over 1,000 citations (Bioinformatics 2015 paper); 250,000 conda installs
tradeoffs: Implements an important subset of samtools (view, index, sort, markdup, depth); GPL; wins depend on spare cores since parallel reading and writing is the mechanism.
caveats: The numbers come from an independent CRG comparison pipeline (guigolab/sambamBench-nf) whose report page I could not open, so they are quoted from the README. The README says samtools 1.4 (March 2017) already reached parity in many areas and the original 2012-2015 advantage was parallel BAM I/O. Samtools wins sort in general. Mostly a parallelism effect, not a D-versus-C one.
why_faster: README: when sambamba started in 2012 its main advantage over samtools was parallelized BAM reading and writing.

name: mistral.rs (Rust LLM inference engine, CUDA)
baseline: llama.cpp (GGUF Q8_0 and Q4_K_M, llama-bench -ngl 99 -fa 1, CUDA backend); report also compares vLLM BF16
workload: Gemma 4 E4B and 26B-A4B prefill and decode tokens per second at prompt lengths and decode depths of 128 to 16384, 256 generated tokens, 1 warmup and 3 measured iterations, on NVIDIA GB10, B200 and H100 SXM.
claimed_speedup: Gemma 4 E4B Q8 (UQFF) vs llama.cpp GGUF Q8_0, report headline: prefill 1.382x-2.113x on GB10 and 1.246x-2.793x on B200, decode 1.086x-1.097x (GB10) and 1.210x-1.263x (B200); mean prefill 1.828x (GB10) and 2.194x (B200), mean decode 1.090x and 1.242x. The report appendix also covers Gemma 4 26B-A4B and H100 SXM.
compiler_and_flags: mistral.rs release v0.8.2 (commit 8b49f963, branch cuda_graphs_v1) built with cargo release and features cuda,cudnn,flash-attn,cutile, rustc 1.96.0 on the H100 host; llama.cpp commit 751ebd17 with llama-bench -ngl 99 -fa 1 (llama.cpp build flags not stated).
hardware: NVIDIA GB10 (driver 580.126.09), NVIDIA B200 (CUDA 13.0, driver 580.126.20), NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 SXM (CUDA 12.8, driver 570.124.06)
tradeoffs: GPU inference through CUDA; uses its own UQFF quantization format for the Q4/Q8 rows; the README table shows near parity for 26B-A4B decode against llama.cpp (46.8 vs 46.4 tok/s on GB10) and mistral.rs behind vLLM BF16 on 26B-A4B prefill (592.2 vs 3878.6 tok/s on GB10).
caveats: GPU-bound workload: gains come from CUDA kernels, paged attention and CUDA graphs rather than from Rust versus C++. UQFF q8 versus GGUF Q8_0 are different quantizations. llama.cpp and vLLM rows were copied from a 2026-05-31 sweep while mistral.rs rows were rerun on 2026-06-01. First-party; llama.cpp build flags unstated, so not tier A.
found_via: GitHub: scan of Rust LLM engines after a Zig topic search turned up fucina; mistral.rs README Benchmarks section and releases/v0.8.2/report.md
why_faster: README: paged-attention and MoE optimizations (plus CUDA graphs on the benchmarked branch); no Rust-specific mechanism is claimed.

name: libbzip2-rs (libbz2-rs-sys, Rust port of libbzip2)
workload: CPU cycles for compression at levels 1-9 on silesia-small.tar and a small sample file, and decompression of bzip2 test files, comparing the C and Rust builds in one harness (bzip2_benchmarks.json).
claimed_speedup: From the Trifecta Tech blog as quoted in a search snippet (page blocked): compression CPU-cycle deltas of -14.87% (sample3.ref, level 1), -14.30% (silesia-small.tar, level 1) and -9.66% (silesia-small.tar, level 9); decompression 'significant speedups across the board'; an independent test on an M1 Linux laptop measured about 4% faster decompression.
stars_or_usage: 79 stars; libbz2-rs-sys has 42.7M crates.io downloads and is the default backend of the bzip2 crate since 0.6
tradeoffs: Drop-in libbzip2 C API (cdylib) and Rust crate; memory-safe translation; project page says no further feature development is planned.
caveats: Snippet only: the percentages come from a search snippet of the blocked blog post, not from a page I opened; the repo holds the benchmark command list but no results. Hardware, compiler and flags unknown. The port started as a c2rust translation of libbzip2, so the gain comes from implementation changes, not a new algorithm. License is the bzip2 license (SPDX bzip2-1.0.6 per crates.io).
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rust library faster than C implementation' then 'libbzip2-rs libbz2-rs-sys faster than C libbzip2 benchmark'

name: ixy network driver in Rust (C2Rust-transpiled unsafe build versus C)
baseline: ixy C user-space network driver packet forwarder (gcc, and clang with the same LLVM version)
workload: CPU cycles and instructions per forwarded 64-byte packet by the ixy forwarder at batch sizes 32 and 8 on an Intel 82599-class NIC, measured with CPU performance counters (paper: The Case for Writing Network Drivers in High-Level Programming Languages, ANCS 2019).
claimed_speedup: C2Rust-transpiled unsafe Rust forwards a packet in 91 cycles with 121 instructions against 94 cycles and 127 instructions for C at batch 32 (about 3% fewer cycles), also true when C is built with clang on the same LLVM version. The idiomatic safe Rust driver is slower: 100 vs 94 cycles (6%) at batch 32 and 120 vs 108 (11%) at batch 8.
hardware: Intel Xeon E3-1230 v3 per the Rust-vs-C document (the repo README names an E3-1230 v2 at 3.3 GHz for the throughput graphs)
tradeoffs: Faster variant is entirely unsafe transpiled Rust without bounds checks; the safe idiomatic driver pays about 65% more instructions that out-of-order execution mostly hides.
caveats: The 'Rust is faster than C (unless you want safety)' line is tongue-in-cheek and rests on a 3-cycle difference from one machine; compiler versions and flags are not stated in the pages I read, and the document says the C code 'didn't use the CPU to its full potential' without naming a mechanism. Hardware generation is inconsistent between the document and the README. Results are from the 2018-2019 paper era and the repo has been quiet since December 2022.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rust rewrite outperforms original C implementation benchmark' surfaced ixy-languages/Rust-vs-C-performance.md
why_faster: Document reports fewer executed instructions per packet in the transpiled build (121 vs 127) but gives no deeper mechanism; for safe Rust it explains that out-of-order CPUs hide bounds-check overhead (IPC 2.09 vs 1.35).

name: zipir (Zig streaming DEFLATE-family compression library and CLI)
baseline: zlib-ng 2.3.3 (zlib and raw DEFLATE), ISA-L igzip, and bgzip with libdeflate 1.26 or zlib-ng (htslib 1.24)
workload: Single-threaded compression at levels 1/5/9 and decompression of gzip, zlib, raw DEFLATE and BGZF on FASTQ (57.2 MB and 20.2 MB), PRIDE XML, mzIdentML and Canterbury tar files, with output size reported beside speed.
claimed_speedup: zlib and raw DEFLATE decompression: zipir is the fastest tool, the fastest peer (zlib-ng) takes 1.24x its time (1.17-1.28x); zlib/raw DEFLATE compression: zlib-ng takes 1.35x zipir's time with 34% larger output at level 1, 1.08x with 2% larger at level 5 and 2.01x with 2% larger at level 9; gzip decompression level with ISA-L igzip (1.01x average, per-file 0.81-1.25); losses: bgzip+libdeflate is 1.07x faster on BGZF decompression and ISA-L igzip is faster at every gzip compression level (with 15-22% larger output).
compiler_and_flags: zipir 0.1.2 built with Zig 0.16.0 ReleaseFast -Dcpu=native, stripped, single-threaded; peers: zlib-ng 2.3.3 and libdeflate 1.26 as static libraries (bioconda configuration), htslib 1.24 default compiler flags with native-instruction codec libraries, ISA-L igzip.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (AVX2), Linux 7.2.7 (Fedora 44), one host, measured 2026-09-27
tradeoffs: Streaming library with fixed caller-owned memory (peak 0.55-0.62 MiB versus 1.6-5.0 MiB for the C tools); no dependencies; compression levels are zipir's own, so output sizes differ from zlib-ng at the same numeric level.
caveats: Report states it predates the current release: compression rows were measured at commit 5f25547 (marked with uncommitted changes) and decompression rows at ff8e9e8. Single host, first-party. Level numbers are not equivalent effort across tools, which is why output size is shown; the loses against ISA-L and libdeflate are documented in the same report. Very new repository.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/bioinformatics?l=zig topic page (same author as z-fasta)

name: bzip2z (Zig bzip2 with SA-IS block sorting)
baseline: system bzip2 1.0.8 (C); pbzip2 1.1.13 reported as a third column
workload: Compression and decompression throughput of a 1.0 MB mixed-pattern buffer with the bundled bench-bzip2 tool, 3 iterations, single thread and 16 resolved threads.
claimed_speedup: Single thread: compress 18.64 vs 10.43 MB/s (1.79x), decompress 67.14 vs 69.38 MB/s (0.97x), output 265768 vs 265931 bytes; with threads=auto (16): compress 27.18 vs 10.33 MB/s (2.63x), decompress 68.65 vs 69.16 MB/s (0.99x).
compiler_and_flags: bzip2z: Zig 0.15.2, -Doptimize=ReleaseFast; system bzip2 1.0.8 and pbzip2 1.1.13 from a Nix dev shell (build flags not stated)
hardware: Apple M4 Max, Darwin 25.3.0 arm64, run 2026-01-15
tradeoffs: Library with C FFI plus a bzip2-compatible CLI; optional multi-stream (pbzip2-style) mode; clean-room rewrite so conformance is the main risk.
caveats: One 1 MB input pattern and three iterations; decompression is parity. The compression win comes from replacing bzip2's block sort with SA-IS, so outputs are not byte-identical to bzip2 and the gain is algorithmic. The threads=auto row adds parallel block compression that stock bzip2 lacks. First-party.
why_faster: README: SA-IS linear-time suffix array construction for the Burrows-Wheeler transform in place of bzip2's original block-sorting logic, plus optional concurrent block compression.

name: rasusa (Rust read and alignment subsampler)
baseline: seqtk sample (C) for random read subsampling; filtlong (C++) for target-bases selection
workload: Subsampling a 2.9 GB single FASTQ (379,547 long reads) to 50x coverage of a 4.4 Mbp genome against filtlong, and paired-end 179 MB files (283,590 reads each) down to 140,000 reads against seqtk sample, via hyperfine.
claimed_speedup: rasusa reads ran 34.91 +/- 0.93 times faster than filtlong (0.740 s vs 25.840 s); paired end: 1.19 times faster than seqtk sample one pass (0.950 s vs 1.132 s) and 1.01 times faster than seqtk two pass (0.963 s).
compiler_and_flags: rasusa target/release build (cargo release); hyperfine --warmup 3 --runs 10 (single) and --warmup 10 --runs 100 (paired); seqtk and filtlong versions and flags not stated.
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner (CPU model not stated); tables regenerated on each release by benches/update_readme.sh
tradeoffs: Subsamples to a coverage or base target without needing a fixed read count; reads and aln modes; supports paired reads.
caveats: filtlong solves a different, quality-aware selection problem, so the 34.9x figure is not like-for-like; against seqtk the same-job gain is 1.01-1.19x, near parity. Shared-runner noise, first-party, tool versions unstated.

name: ziggit (Zig git reimplementation)
baseline: git (C) CLI: status, log -20, branch -a, blame
workload: hyperfine (100 runs, 5 warmups) of small git commands in a test repository on macOS arm64, plus in-process library calls versus spawning git as a subprocess for a bun-style workflow.
claimed_speedup: README: 4-10x faster than git on macOS arm64: status 8.1 ms vs 1.0 ms (8.1x), log -20 8.4 vs 1.7 ms (5.0x), branch -a 7.9 vs 1.4 ms (5.6x), blame on a large repo 36 vs 2.8 ms (12.6x); as a library: findCommit 85x (macOS arm64) and 6x (Linux x86_64), cloneBare 7x and 34x, full workflow 10x and 32x.
compiler_and_flags: Zig ReleaseFast builds (7.5 MB on macOS arm64); git version and build flags not stated; the README links BENCHMARKS.md which I could not open (404 at the default branch path); benchmark sources are in benchmarks/*.zig
hardware: macOS arm64 (CPU model not stated); Linux x86_64 for some library rows
tradeoffs: Drop-in git CLI plus Zig library, WASM build (142 KB), built-in git server and a succinct output mode for LLM use; GPL-2.0; feature parity with git tracked through git's own test suite results.
caveats: Sub-10 ms commands on small repositories are dominated by process start and file-system latency, so the multipliers say little about throughput on large repositories; the library rows measure in-process calls against spawning a subprocess, an overhead difference not an algorithm difference; git version unspecified; first-party.
found_via: WebSearch: 'pure Zig implementation benchmark faster than C reference library' (github.com results)

name: zog (Zig SIMD JSONL search engine)
baseline: jq (C); the README column is labelled jq/jaq and also lists ripgrep
workload: Queries over a 1 GB JSONL dataset (6.7 million lines): key match, substring match, numeric comparison, TSV field extraction, JSON reformatting, aggregation and OR/AND logic, in GB/s.
claimed_speedup: zog (file) 4.03 GB/s simple key match vs 0.07 GB/s for jq/jaq, 2.83 GB/s field extraction vs 0.10, 2.41 GB/s aggregation vs 0.05; 20-50x faster than jq/jaq for typical queries; also faster than ripgrep (2.30 GB/s) and 4.1x faster on complex logic (2.24 vs 0.54 GB/s).
compiler_and_flags: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast; jq, jaq and ripgrep versions and flags not stated
hardware: 'modern NVMe SSD' only; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Does not fully parse JSON: byte-level SIMD key scanning in 8 MB blocks with a background reader thread, so malformed JSON and escaped keys may behave differently from jq; narrower query language.
caveats: First-party numbers with no versions, flags or CPU. jq and jaq (Rust) share one column so the C baseline alone is not separable. zog does a different, lighter job than jq (no AST, no validation), so the multiplier compares different semantics.
why_faster: README: skips building an AST (jq bottlenecks near 0.04 GB/s on it) and scans 32-byte chunks with AVX2/NEON bitmasks while a producer thread reads the next 8 MB block.

name: ZLB (Zig Language Benchmark) Mandelbrot SIMD row
baseline: C Mandelbrot with 4-lane SIMD intrinsics, gcc 16.1.1 and clang 22.1.8 at -O3 -march=native -ffp-contract=off (also zig cc)
workload: Mandelbrot set calculation, hyperfine mean of 20 runs after 1 warmup, wall-time ratio against the scalar gcc build (1.00x).
claimed_speedup: Time ratio vs scalar gcc: zig_simd_fast 0.16x and zig_simd_safe 0.18x against c_simd_clang 0.26x, c_simd_gcc 0.27x, rust_simd 0.27x, c_simd_zigcc 0.27x (Zig SIMD about 1.6-1.7x faster than the C SIMD builds); scalar rows are parity (zig_std_fast 1.00x, c_std_gcc 1.00x, c_std_clang 1.02x). Other rows in the same suite: sieve zig_static_bitset_fast 0.63x vs c_std_gcc 1.00x, btree zig_compact_fast 0.19x vs c_arena_gcc 0.21x, log_proc zig_std_fast 0.83x vs c_std_gcc 1.00x.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0 zig build-exe -O ReleaseFast (native CPU, README says -mcpu=native); C: gcc 16.1.1 and clang 22.1.8 with -O3, SIMD C rows add -march=native -ffp-contract=off, scalar C rows use -O3 only (Makefile read); Rust 1.97.1 opt-level=3 with LTO
tradeoffs: Informal suite of five small benchmarks (mandel, sieve, btree, log_proc, atomics) in Zig, C, Rust, Go, Python and Bash.
caveats: Not like-for-like: the Zig SIMD kernel uses 8-lane f64 vectors while the C and Rust SIMD kernels use 4-lane intrinsics, scalar C rows lack -march=native while Zig builds natively, and the sieve and btree wins come from different data layouts (bitset, 32-bit indices), not the language. Single commit, single unnamed machine.
found_via: WebSearch: 'written in Zig faster than C library benchmark' (zff.dev mirror of tsukumoakito/zlb), then github.com/topics/benchmark?l=zig
why_faster: Source: Zig's @Vector with 8-lane f64 fills the CPU's execution units better than the 4-lane intrinsics used in C and Rust, and gives LLVM clearer intent.
